title: Honeycomb (cinder toffee)
subtitle: homemade honeycomb candy with a crisp caramel and airy texture
excerpt: Honeycomb is a caramel-based confectionery that turns from a dense toffee syrup to a crisp, bubbly candy when bicarbonate of soda is stirred in at the last moment. The texture is light and airy, with an intensely sweet caramel flavour. The most important step is reaching exactly 150 degrees Celsius before removing from the heat, as a few degrees either way changes the texture dramatically.
sourceNotes: Traditional British confectionery, documented in various 19th and 20th-century household baking manuals (public domain). Mrs Beeton (Book of Household Management, 1861, public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar cooking stage reached at 149 to 154 degrees Celsius, at which the syrup sets rigid and brittle when cooled. Used for pulled sugar, lollipops, and honeycomb.
The browning reaction that occurs when sugar is heated above 160 degrees Celsius, producing complex bitter-sweet flavour compounds and a deep amber colour.
A chemical raising agent that reacts with heat and acids to produce carbon dioxide bubbles. In honeycomb it is added to hot caramel to create the characteristic airy, porous texture.

content.text: Honeycomb is sugar syrup taken to
hard crack stage
, then puffed up with
bicarbonate of soda
. The
caramelisation
at 150°C gives the finished slab its amber colour and bittersweet flavour. A thermometer is not optional. A few degrees separates crisp honeycomb from sticky toffee.
If hot syrup touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes and seek medical care if needed.
Method
Prepare the tin
Line a deep baking tray with a baking mat or well-oiled baking parchment. Place it on a heatproof surface close to the hob. Once poured, honeycomb cannot be moved until fully set.
Making the caramel
Put the caster sugar and golden syrup into a medium saucepan. Set over a medium heat and stir gently until the sugar has dissolved completely. Stop stirring once dissolved.

Clip the sugar thermometer to the inside of the pan. Increase the heat to medium-high and bring to a boil without stirring. Cook until the thermometer reads exactly 150 degrees Celsius. The syrup will turn a deep amber at this temperature.
Remove from the heat the moment the thermometer hits 150 degrees. The residual heat in the pan will continue to cook the syrup briefly, so do not wait.
Adding bicarbonate of soda
Tip in the bicarbonate of soda in one go. Using a silicone spatula, stir swiftly for just 3 to 4 seconds: enough to fully combine, but no more. The mixture will foam up dramatically.
Immediately pour the foaming mixture into the prepared tray. Do not spread or press it: let it settle naturally or the bubbles will deflate and the honeycomb will be dense rather than airy.
Setting and breaking
Leave the honeycomb to set at room temperature for at least 60 minutes. Do not refrigerate: condensation will make the surface sticky.

Once fully set and cold, break the honeycomb into irregular pieces by pressing firmly with the back of a wooden spoon or the flat of a palette knife. The candy should snap cleanly. If it bends rather than snaps, it has not set fully.
Storing

Transfer immediately to an airtight container. Honeycomb absorbs moisture from the air and will become sticky and soft if left uncovered even for a short time. Store at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.

attrs.problem: Honeycomb is chewy rather than crisp
attrs.avoid: Avoid removing the syrup from the heat before it reaches 150 degrees Celsius.
attrs.fix: Use a calibrated sugar thermometer and wait until the reading is stable at 150 before adding the bicarbonate of soda.

attrs.problem: Honeycomb is dense with few bubbles
attrs.avoid: Avoid over-stirring after adding the bicarbonate of soda; more than 4 or 5 strokes collapses the foam.
attrs.fix: Stir just enough to fully incorporate the bicarbonate, then pour immediately without any further manipulation.

attrs.avoid: Avoid storing in the refrigerator or leaving uncovered at room temperature.
attrs.fix: Transfer to an airtight container as soon as the honeycomb is broken. Humidity is the main cause of stickiness.

attrs.problem: Syrup burns and turns very dark or bitter
attrs.avoid: Avoid leaving the pan unattended at high heat; the syrup rises from 140 to 160 degrees quickly.
attrs.fix: Watch the thermometer continuously for the last 10 degrees. If the syrup is very dark and smells burnt, discard it and start again.
